newsitem.title: MALTA: Arabs plan strategy for talks attended by Israelis.
newsitem.headline: Arabs plan strategy for talks attended by Israelis.

text.p: Arab officials, urging Europe to take a tougher line against Israeli settlements in East Jerusalem, were to meet on Tuesday to plan strategy before a conference attended by Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy.

The conference later in the day will bring Palestinians led by President Yasser Aarafat and Israelis together for the first time since building work on a settlement in East Jerusalem threw the Middle East peace process into disarray a month ago.

Late on Monday, Palestinian Planning and International Cooperation Minister Nabil Shaath told reporters: "There are no arrangements for an Arafat-Levy meeting at this stage but the Europeans are trying to bring about progress...it depends on the willingness of the Israeli side to respond."
Shaath made his comments before going for talks with European Union council of ministers chairman Hans van Mierlo in a hotel in the Maltese capital, Valletta.
Earlier, Palestinian spokesman Nabil Abu Rdainah also said Levy and Arafat would not meet in Malta but that Shaath might have talks with the Israeli minister.

The Arab group meeting is meant to focus on the agenda for the two-day EU-Mediterranean conference -- a followup to the partnership forged between 15 European Union countries and 12 south Mediterranean partners in Barcelona 1995.

Egyptian Foreign Minister Amra Moussa said the group would meet "to discuss and coordinate our policies vis a vis the agenda of the meeting -- relations within the Barcelona process, the economic, political and agriculture sides".
But he admitted that while the Middle East was not on the agenda "it is there, looming in the air. It is in the climate, it's in the atmosphere and we, the Mediterraneans, cannot not be affected".
Delegates said Arab foreign ministers might hold their own meeting after that of the officials and before the conference.
Earlier, a European source told Reuters that work on the draft declaration to be submitted to the foreign ministers had been delayed by concerns over the Middle East.
"The main dispute is over the peace process. The text repeated the Barcelona declaration. The Arabs want to take it further with a reference to Israeli settlements," he said.
But the fact that Israelis and Palestinians will be at the same venue is seen by some delegates and officials as progress.

European Union Commission vice-president Manuel Marin described it as "good news". As late as Monday, there had been doubts over whether Levy would attend a session in which some Israelis feared he could be pilloried.

Diplomats say the Europeans had wanted to keep the crisis in Middle East talks in the background and concentrate on the long- term economic and security relationship between the northern and southern shores of the Mediterranean.
But for the Arabs, the Middle East peace process is an inevitable part of any security and economic relationships.
The Europeans appear to have accepted that the Middle East will loom large but are seeking damage-limitation, as evidence of some discord surfaced.
Malta's coordinator Paul Mifsud told a news briefing that general statements by ministers, originally planned to be broadcast live, might now not be. He would not give a reason.
The Arabs, especially those in the eastern Mediterranean, argue that any debate on security cannot ignore Israel's attitude in the Middle East peace talks.

"The Arab concept is linked to developments in the Middle East peace process, because a bigger threat to security and stability comes from what is happening there," said Algerian Foreign Minister Ahmed Attaf, coordinator of the Arab group.
